explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Eliphaz asks if a wise man would 'argue with useless words or speeches that serve no purpose' (Job 15:3). In plain words, he's calling Job's talk empty. I think the hot east wind is his picture of all noise and nothing to show for it. That's a rough review for a friend who came to comfort him (Job 2:11).

Nobody's calling Job soft here, friend. Eliphaz says a wise man wouldn't use 'useless words or speeches that serve no purpose' (Job 15:3). Gentle does show up later, when he asks about 'words spoken gently to you' (Job 15:11), but that's a different question. In verse 3 he's talking about what Job's words are worth.

Length never comes up, baker. Eliphaz says a wise man wouldn't use 'useless words or speeches that serve no purpose' (Job 15:3). His complaint is about what the words are worth, not how many there are. And with 35 verses in this chapter, short isn't exactly Eliphaz's style.

Mouth it is. Eliphaz says, 'Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you' (Job 15:6). Notice he doesn't stop at the mouth, because the lips get called to testify too. That's two witnesses, and both of them are Job's.

Hands don't make the cut in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says, 'Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you' (Job 15:6). He's pointing at Job's words. Hands do show up later in the chapter, when the wicked man 'has stretched out his hand against God' (Job 15:25), but that's a different part of the speech.

Feet don't get a word in, baker. Eliphaz says, 'Your own mouth, not mine, condemns you; your own lips testify against you' (Job 15:6). The mouth and the lips are the ones on the stand. Two witnesses, and neither one is a toe.

That's the point, baker. Eliphaz asks, 'What do you know that we do not? What do you understand that is not clear to us?' (Job 15:9). I think he's saying Job has no secret knowledge the three of them lack. He fires it off as questions, like a man who isn't waiting for an answer.

explanations.answer: Job is older than all of them
explanations.explanation: Eliphaz actually goes the other direction, friend. He asks, 'Were you the first man ever born?' (Job 15:7), and he says the gray-haired men on their side are 'men much older than your father' (Job 15:10). He isn't saying Job is the oldest in the room. Verse 9 is about what Job knows that they don't.

Prayer schedules aren't in these verses, baker. Eliphaz asks, 'Do you listen in on the council of God or limit wisdom to yourself?' (Job 15:8). Then he adds, 'What do you know that we do not?' (Job 15:9). Both questions are about knowledge, not how often Job prays.

True, baker. Eliphaz says the gray-haired and the aged are on their side, 'men much older than your father' (Job 15:10). That's a whole lot of birthdays on one team. He's counting years the way I count chocolate chips.

The text says the opposite, friend. Eliphaz says the gray-haired and the aged on their side are 'men much older than your father' (Job 15:10). So these men have more years behind them than Job's own father. That's a whole lot of birthdays on one side of the argument.

That's what Eliphaz says, baker. He asks why Job's heart has carried him away and why his eyes flash, 'so that you turn your spirit against God and pour such words from your mouth?' (Job 15:12-13). That's his accusation. Heart, eyes, spirit and mouth, and the whole body's in on it.

Hiding isn't in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says Job's eyes flash, and that he turns his spirit 'against God and pour such words from your mouth' (Job 15:12-13). Flashing eyes and pouring words don't sound much like hiding to me. That's the accusation Eliphaz is making.

Running isn't what Eliphaz describes, baker. He says Job turns his spirit 'against God and pour such words from your mouth' (Job 15:13). Someone running away isn't usually pouring words out of his mouth. Eliphaz is talking about Job's words and what's behind them.

Eliphaz says the opposite, friend. He says, 'If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes…' (Job 15:15). Notice the 'if,' and notice it's Eliphaz speaking. He's heading toward 'how much less man' in the next verse (Job 15:16). Even the heavens get called out in this speech.

That's right, baker. Eliphaz says, 'If God puts no trust in His holy ones, if even the heavens are not pure in His eyes' (Job 15:15). Not complete trust, but none. That 'if' matters, because it's Eliphaz speaking, and he uses it to get to 'how much less man' (Job 15:16).

Injustice is the word. Eliphaz says man is 'vile and corrupt, who drinks injustice like water' (Job 15:16). I think water is his picture of something taken in all day, without a second thought. That's how he describes man, in his own words.

Kindness doesn't fit his sentence, friend. Eliphaz says man 'drinks injustice like water' (Job 15:16). Just before that, he calls man 'vile and corrupt.' So kindness isn't what he's pouring into the cup.

Wisdom would be a nice pour, baker, but it's not in this verse. Eliphaz says man 'drinks injustice like water' (Job 15:16). Wisdom does appear earlier in the speech, where he asks if Job limits 'wisdom to himself' (Job 15:8). That's a different question from this one.

That's him, baker. Eliphaz starts with, 'A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless' (Job 15:20). He's passing along what wise men declared (Job 15:17-18). And he picks one topic and sticks to it like dough on a rolling pin.

No faithful servant in this stretch, friend. Eliphaz begins with, 'A wicked man writhes in pain all his days' (Job 15:20). From there he stays with the wicked, the ruthless and the godless, all the way to verse 35. If you were hoping he'd switch topics, he doesn't.

No widow in these verses, baker. Eliphaz starts with, 'A wicked man writhes in pain all his days; only a few years are reserved for the ruthless' (Job 15:20). The speech sounds heavy enough to be about grief, I'll give you that. But the one he's describing is the wicked man.

Eliphaz says the opposite, friend. He says, 'in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him' (Job 15:21). So it comes while the man is prospering, not after he's lost it. Terrible timing, and that's how Eliphaz paints it.

That's right, baker. Eliphaz says, 'in his prosperity the destroyer attacks him' (Job 15:21). It hits while the man is prospering, not after he's poor. Money in the account and terror in the ears, all at once.

explanations.answer: Stretched out his hand against God
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Eliphaz says, 'he has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty' (Job 15:25). After five verses of what happens to the wicked man, here's the 'because.' It's the reason Eliphaz gives.

Offerings don't come up in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says the man 'has stretched out his hand against God' (Job 15:25). The charge he names is aimed at God Himself. It's not a missed-deadline kind of accusation.

Servants aren't in this verse, baker. Eliphaz says the man 'has stretched out his hand against God and has vaunted himself against the Almighty' (Job 15:25). Both halves point at God. That's the reason Eliphaz gives.
True, baker. Eliphaz says the wicked man is 'rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield' (Job 15:26). The 'Him' is God, from the verse before. Picture it: head down, shield up, no brakes.

The text says he does, friend. Eliphaz says the man is 'rushing headlong at Him with a thick, studded shield' (Job 15:26). The 'Him' is God, from verse 25. So it's a full charge, and he's armored up for it.

Ruined is the word, baker. Eliphaz says, 'he will dwell in ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble' (Job 15:28). That's the picture he paints for the wicked man's home. Not a listing anybody's lining up for.

Royal would be a big upgrade, friend, but that's not the verse. Eliphaz says 'ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble' (Job 15:28). A king does show up in this chapter, but as a picture of distress, which overwhelms the man 'like a king poised to attack' (Job 15:24).

Holy isn't in this verse, baker. Eliphaz says 'ruined cities, in abandoned houses destined to become rubble' (Job 15:28). The only holy in this chapter is earlier, where he talks about God's 'holy ones' (Job 15:15). Different part of the speech.

Eliphaz says no, friend. He says, 'He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure' (Job 15:29). Then he adds that the man's possessions 'will not overspread the land.' No investment tips in this speech.

That's right, baker. Eliphaz says, 'He will no longer be rich; his wealth will not endure' (Job 15:29). He also says the man's possessions 'will not overspread the land.' In Eliphaz's picture, the money doesn't last.

Emptiness is the word. Eliphaz says, 'Let him not deceive himself with trust in emptiness, for emptiness will be his reward' (Job 15:31). I think the picture is trusting in nothing and getting nothing back. It's an empty cookie box with a very nice lid.

Riches are off the table, friend. Eliphaz says, 'emptiness will be his reward' (Job 15:31). Two verses earlier he says, 'He will no longer be rich' (Job 15:29). So the reward he names is empty-handed.
Honor isn't on the list, baker. Eliphaz says, 'emptiness will be his reward' (Job 15:31). It's a reward, but not the kind anyone puts on a shelf. That's one trophy nobody's asking for.

That's his point, baker. Eliphaz says, 'his branch will not flourish' (Job 15:32). Then he pictures 'a vine stripped of its unripe grapes, like an olive tree that sheds its blossoms' (Job 15:33). Anyone who has watched a houseplant lose its leaves knows that sad look.
No comeback story here, friend. Eliphaz says, 'his branch will not flourish' (Job 15:32). The vine is stripped and the olive tree sheds its blossoms (Job 15:33). Nothing in these verses grows back.

Feeding people isn't the picture, baker. Eliphaz says, 'his branch will not flourish' (Job 15:32). His vine is stripped of its unripe grapes and his olive tree sheds its blossoms (Job 15:33). Even a cookie guy like me can tell that's not a harvest to share.

Evil is the word, baker. Eliphaz says, 'They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit' (Job 15:35). Trouble goes in and evil comes out. That's how he closes his speech.
Peace is the opposite of this line, friend. Eliphaz says, 'They conceive trouble and give birth to evil' (Job 15:35). Peace isn't anywhere in the picture. He ends on 'deceit.'

Mercy doesn't appear in this verse, baker. Eliphaz says, 'They conceive trouble and give birth to evil; their womb is pregnant with deceit' (Job 15:35). It's a heavy line to end on. Mercy isn't what comes out of it.
